## Animations

### The question

Waves in shallow water are usually modeled by the shallow water (Saint-Venant)
equations, which track the water depth and the depth-averaged velocity.  Over
a flat bottom, these equations predict that any hump of water eventually
steepens until its front becomes vertical, like a breaking wave.  After that,
the hump spreads into a triangular shape (an "N-wave") and slowly decays.

What happens if the bottom is not flat but has a repeating pattern of
ridges and troughs?  In these animations the bottom alternates between
depths of 1 m and 0.3 m every half meter, and the water starts at rest with a
smooth hump a few centimeters high.  The hump splits into a left-going and a
right-going wave; the animations follow the right-going one.

### Flat versus periodic bottom

The dashed line shows the wave over a flat bottom: its front steepens into a
vertical jump and the wave takes on the triangular N-wave shape.  The solid
line shows the same initial hump over the periodic bottom.  Instead of
breaking, it separates into a series of smooth, separate peaks.

{{< video movies/flat_vs_periodic.mp4 >}}

### Solitary waves

Running the periodic-bottom case longer shows that the peaks keep their
shape and travel at different speeds, with the tallest in front.  Waves like
this, which hold their shape as they travel, are called solitary waves.  They
are typical of *dispersive* wave equations, in which waves of different
lengths travel at different speeds, but the shallow water equations over a
flat bottom are not dispersive.  The periodic bottom supplies the
dispersion.

{{< video movies/pwc_t270.mp4 >}}

### A closer look

The same simulation near the end of the run, with frames much closer
together in time.  On this time scale you can see the wave shapes change
rapidly as they pass over each step in the bottom, and a pattern of small
ripples behind them.

{{< video movies/detailed_short.mp4 >}}

### An effective model

The main result of the paper is a set of *homogenized* equations: equations
with constant coefficients, which no longer involve the detailed shape of
the bottom, but whose solutions approximate the averaged behavior of the
waves.  The derivation produces a series of corrections in powers of
$\delta$, the period of the bottom relative to the length of the waves;
keeping terms up to $\delta^3$ or up to $\delta^5$ gives two versions of the
model.  Both contain dispersive terms, which explains where the solitary
waves come from.

This animation compares the shallow water solution with the two
homogenized models.  Both match well at first; over time the waves of the
$\delta^3$ model run ahead, while the $\delta^5$ model stays close to the
shallow water solution.  The homogenized equations are also much cheaper to
solve: for this problem the paper reports a speedup of about 200 times.

{{< video movies/compare_35_pwc_t270.mp4 >}}
